intro: We describe people every day: to find someone at the airport, to talk about a colleague, to present a friend. English uses “be” for height and character, and “have got” for hair and eyes.
objectifs: Know the difference between “What does she look like?” (appearance) and “What is she like?” (character).
Describe height, body, age, hair and eyes.
Describe character with common adjectives and avoid false friends.
Build a description with be, have got, wear and with.

sections.titre: Three questions: don't mix them up
texte: “What does he look like?” asks about appearance: “He's tall with short hair.” “What is he like?” asks about character (or a general opinion): “He's very kind.” “How is he?” asks about health and feelings: “He's fine, thanks.”
In “What is he like?”, “like” is not the verb “like” (love). It is a preposition that means “similar to”. The question means “Describe him for me”.

lignes: She's tall and slim. She's got long hair.
She's fine. / She's a bit tired.

exemples: What does your new boss look like? — She's short with grey hair.
What's your new boss like? — She's very patient.

sections.titre: Height, body and age: be + adjective
texte: For height, body and age, use “be” + adjective. Adjectives never take an s: “They're tall”, not “They're talls”.
For exact height, also use “be”: “He's one metre eighty” or “He's 1.80 m (tall)”. In the UK and the USA, people also use feet and inches: “He's six feet tall”.
Be polite: “fat” can hurt people. Say “a bit overweight” or “big”. For an old person, “elderly” is more polite than “old”.

lignes: slim · thin · well-built · a bit overweight
in his twenties · in her forties
pretty: usually women; handsome: usually men

exemples: My brother is tall and slim.
sections.note: “Short” is the opposite of “tall” for people, and of “long” for hair. Don't say “He is little” about an adult: say “He's short”.

sections.titre: Hair, eyes and details: have got / wear / with
texte: For hair, eyes and beards, use “have got” or “have”: “She's got brown eyes.” / “She has brown eyes.”
“Hair” (on your head) is uncountable: it stays singular, with no “a” and no s. “Her hair is long.” The plural “hairs” means a few single hairs.
Order of adjectives before “hair”: length, then shape, then colour: “long curly black hair”. Lesson 35 looks at adjective order in more detail.
For clothes and glasses, use “wear”: “He wears glasses.” You can also use “with”: “the woman with red hair”, “a man with a beard”.

lignes: black · brown · fair / blonde · red · grey · white

exemples: He's got short curly black hair.
My grandfather is bald and he has a white beard.
Who's the man with the moustache?
sections.note: No article before “hair” in a description: “She has black hair”, never “She has the black hair”.

texte: For character, use “be” + adjective: “She's kind.” You can add “very”, “quite” (fairly) and “a bit” (a little). We use “a bit” mostly for negative qualities: “He's a bit lazy.”
False friends: “sympathetic” means you understand someone's problems; it does not mean “nice”. “Sensible” means practical and reasonable; a person who cries easily is “sensitive”.

lignes: It's kind of you to help.
My son is shy with new people.

exemples: My colleague is very friendly but a bit shy.
very + quality; a bit + small problem.
Our teacher is quite strict but very funny.

formule: be + height / character (He's tall and kind) · have got + hair / eyes (He's got short black hair) · wear glasses
prononciation: “hair” /heə/ and “her” /hɜː/ are different: “hair” sounds like “air” with an h. Breathe out for the h.
“eyes” /aɪz/ sounds like “I's”; the final s is /z/.
“moustache” is /məˈstɑːʃ/ in British English, with the stress on the second syllable.
“What does she look like?”: stress LOOK and LIKE; “does” is weak /dəz/.
erreurs: He has blue eyes and blonds hairs.
He has blue eyes and blond hair.
“Hair” is uncountable; adjectives never take an s.
She is very sympathetic. (meaning nice)
She's very nice. / She's very friendly.
“Sympathetic” means understanding someone's problems.
How is your brother? — He's tall and slim.
What does your brother look like? — He's tall and slim.
“How is he?” asks about health; for appearance: “What does he look like?”.
She has the long hair.
She has long hair.
No article before “hair” in a description.
He has long hair black.
He has long black hair.
Adjectives go before the noun: length + colour + hair.
He measures 1.80 m.
He's 1.80 m tall. / He's one metre eighty.
Use “be” for a person's height.
My sister is very sensible, she cries at every film.
My sister is very sensitive.
sensible = reasonable; sensitive = easily upset or touched.
What is like your sister?
What is your sister like?
“Like” goes at the end of the question.

dialogue.contexte: Marc must meet his wife's cousin at Montreal airport. He has never seen her.
lignes: What does your cousin look like? I don't know her.
She's quite tall and slim, and she's got long curly black hair.
Yes, big red glasses. And she's in her twenties.
OK. And what's she like? I'm a bit nervous.
Don't worry, she's really friendly and very funny. She's a bit chatty!
Great. So: a tall woman with red glasses and curly hair.
Exactly. Her name is Fatou. Here's her number.

mots: with a lot of curls, not straight
My uncle has a grey beard.
hair on a man's chin and face
two pieces of glass you wear to see better
nice and kind to other people
nervous with people you don't know

exercices.consigne: Which question goes with the answer: “What does he/she look like?” or “What is he/she like?”?
Put the words in the right order to make a sentence.
Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: My neighbour is very nice. / My neighbour is very friendly.
He has forty years more or less.
The man of the beard is my uncle.
The man with the beard is my uncle.

exercices.consigne: Describe a person you know well: appearance (height, hair, eyes) and character, in four or five sentences.
items: My best friend is called Samuel. He's in his thirties. He's tall and well-built, and he's got short black hair and brown eyes. He wears glasses. He's very kind and funny, but he's a bit lazy!

a_retenir: What does she look like? = appearance; What is she like? = character; How is she? = health.
be + height, age, character: She's tall, young and friendly.
have got + hair / eyes: He's got short curly black hair (length, shape, colour). “Hair” stays singular, with no article.
wear glasses; the man with a beard.
False friends: nice / friendly (not “sympathetic”); sensitive (not “sensible”) for a person who is easily upset.
